items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: And today, Billy Cobham, Steve Gadd, Tony Williams, a lot of these guys are composing and writing

ctx.x: Oh — a drummer knows that, yes.

Well a lot of the young drummers, well some of the older guys like Tiny Kahn was a great orchestrator, great arranger. And today, Billy Cobham, Steve Gadd, Tony Williams, a lot of these guys are composing and writing, and Harvey Mason, drummers like that you know, not only great percussion players but they’re very sensitive as to what the music is all about.
And when was it that you really felt that you could become a professional musician?

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The last time I saw him, he said, “I’m getting two bass drums.” I said, “Don’t do it. You don’t need it.”

ctx.x: We didn’t talk about Tony Williams yesterday. You were talking all the – a lot of drummers, but Tony Williams’s name didn’t come up. Do you want to talk about Tony now and why you included him?

Yeah. The guy was a natural player, original. The last time I saw him, he said, “I’m getting two bass drums.” I said, “Don’t do it. You don’t need it.” He was – like Elvin Jones, he added something new to the drum set. He had another voice going. Tremendous.
How would you describe what was distinctive about his style or his approach, Tony Williams?
